CHAPTER 3.1 · LEARNING AREA 3

CHAPTER 3.1 · LEARNING AREA 3 · JANUARY

Angles and triangles

Where two straight lines cross, four angles are formed – and two of them already determine all the others. In every triangle the three angles add up to 180°. You learn the angle theorems, sort triangles by their sides and angles, and find out when a triangle can be constructed uniquely.

15 LESSONS3 UNITS3 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • recognise and calculate adjacent angles, vertically opposite angles, corresponding angles and alternate angles
  • justify and apply the angle sum theorem
  • classify triangles by their angles and sides
  • construct triangles with the congruence theorems and check the triangle inequality

180°

90°

How many degrees does a full angle have?

360°

UNIT 15 LESSONS

1Angles at lines

Two straight lines cross. One angle is 50°. Its neighbour on the same line makes it up to 180°: it has 130°. The angle opposite has 50° again. So a single angle gives away all four.

Adjacent angles lie next to each other on a straight line, vertically opposite angles lie opposite each other at the point of intersection. If two parallel lines are cut by a third, the same angles appear at both points of intersection: corresponding angles (same position) and alternate angles (crosswise, Z shape).

KEY POINT · ANGLE THEOREMS

Adjacent angle theorem: adjacent angles add up to 180°.

Vertically opposite angle theorem: vertically opposite angles are equal.

Corresponding and alternate angle theorem: where parallel lines are cut, corresponding angles and alternate angles are equal.

Angles with three points: $\angle ABC$ has its vertex in the middle, that is at $B$.

Only with parallel lines: if the lines are not parallel, corresponding angles are different in size.

INTERACTIVE · ANGLES AT LINES THAT CROSS

Turn the lines. Which angles stay equal? What changes when the two lines are no longer parallel?

EXAMPLE 1 · FOUR ANGLES FROM ONE

Two straight lines cross, and one angle measures 38°. How big are the other three?

Adjacent angle: $180° - 38° = 142°$. Vertically opposite angle: 38°.

142°, 38° and 142°

EXAMPLE 2 · GIVING REASONS

Why are vertically opposite angles always equal?

The vertically opposite angles $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ have the same adjacent angle $\beta$: $\alpha + \beta = 180°$ and $\gamma + \beta = 180°$.

So $\alpha = \gamma$ must hold.

EXERCISES

Two straight lines cross. One angle is a) 70°   b) 115°   c) 90°. Calculate the other three angles.

a) 110°, 70°, 110°   b) 65°, 115°, 65°   c) all 90°

A railway track crosses two parallel roads. At the first road the acute angle is 40°. How big are the acute and the obtuse angle at the second road?

Corresponding angles: acute 40°, obtuse $180° - 40° = 140°$.

An angle is three times as big as its adjacent angle. How big are the two?

Together, 4 equal parts of 180°.

One part is 45°: the angles are 45° and 135°.

A pair of corresponding angles at the lines $g$ and $h$ measures 72° and 75°. What can you say about $g$ and $h$?

They are not parallel, because at parallel lines corresponding angles would be equal.

Two adjacent angles differ by 40°. How big are they? Draw the situation with a set square.

$180° - 40° = 140°$, half of it 70°. The angles are 70° and 110°.

TEST YOURSELF!

An angle measures 50°. How many degrees does its adjacent angle have?

$180° - 50° = 130°$

Where parallel lines are cut, one angle measures 65°. How big is its alternate angle?

Alternate angles are equal: 65°

An angle is three times as big as its adjacent angle. How big is it?

$3 \cdot 45° = 135°$

UNIT 25 LESSONS

2Angle sum theorem and types of triangle

The three torn-off corners of a paper triangle together form a straight angle – always, no matter what the triangle looks like. With alternate angles you can prove it: draw the parallel to $\overline{AB}$ through $C$.

At the parallel through $C$ there is an alternate angle to $\alpha$ on the left and one to $\beta$ on the right, with $\gamma$ in between. Together they form a straight angle.

Triangles are sorted by their largest angle: acute-angled (all below 90°), right-angled (one exactly 90°), obtuse-angled (one above 90°). By their sides: scalene, isosceles (two sides of equal length) or equilateral (three sides of equal length).

KEY POINT · ANGLE SUM THEOREM

In every triangle: $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 180°$

In an isosceles triangle the two base angles are equal. In an equilateral triangle every angle is 60°.

Never two right or obtuse angles: $90° + 90°$ is already 180°, and nothing would be left for the third angle.

Quadrilaterals: a diagonal divides every quadrilateral into two triangles. That is why the angle sum in a quadrilateral is 360°.

INTERACTIVE · THE ANGLE SUM

Drag the corners. The angles change, their sum does not. The parallel through the top vertex shows why.

EXAMPLE 3 · THE THIRD ANGLE

In a triangle, $\alpha = 50°$ and $\beta = 60°$. How big is $\gamma$, and what type of triangle is it?

$\gamma = 180° - 50° - 60° = 70°$. All angles are less than 90°.

$\gamma = 70°$, acute-angled

EXAMPLE 4 · ISOSCELES

A gable is isosceles, and each base angle measures 45°. How big is the angle at the ridge?

$180° - 2 \cdot 45° = 90°$

There is a right angle at the ridge.

EXERCISES

Calculate the missing angle and name the triangle: a) $\alpha = 30°$, $\beta = 60°$   b) $\alpha = 20°$, $\beta = 40°$   c) $\alpha = 70°$, $\gamma = 55°$

a) $\gamma = 90°$, right-angled   b) $\gamma = 120°$, obtuse-angled   c) $\beta = 55°$, acute-angled and isosceles

An isosceles triangle has 50° at the apex. How big is each base angle?

$(180° - 50°) : 2 = 65°$

Lina measures 58°, 64° and 62° in a triangle. What do you say to that?

The sum is 184°. It must be 180°, so at least one measurement is inaccurate.

The angles of a triangle are in the ratio $1 : 2 : 3$. How big are they, and what type of triangle is it?

6 parts are 180°, one part 30°: 30°, 60°, 90°. Right-angled.

A quadrilateral has the angles 80°, 95° and 110°. How big is the fourth angle? Give a reason with the angle sum theorem.

A diagonal divides the quadrilateral into two triangles, so the sum is $2 \cdot 180° = 360°$. The fourth angle: $360° - 285° = 75°$.

TEST YOURSELF!

$\alpha = 50°$, $\beta = 60°$. How big is $\gamma$?

$180° - 110° = 70°$

An isosceles triangle with base angles of 40°. How big is the angle at the apex?

$180° - 80° = 100°$

How big is each angle in an equilateral triangle?

$180° : 3 = 60°$

UNIT 35 LESSONS

3Constructing triangles

Straws of 4 cm, 5 cm and 10 cm do not make a triangle: the two short ones do not reach each other. With 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm it works – and it always comes out the same. So three sides fix a triangle, if there is one at all.

Two triangles that fit exactly on top of each other are called congruent. The congruence theorems say which three parts fix a triangle uniquely.

Before constructing, you draw a sketch and mark the given parts. Then you check: does the triangle exist at all?

KEY POINT · CONGRUENCE THEOREMS AND TRIANGLE INEQUALITY

SSS: three sides · SAS: two sides and the angle between them · ASA: one side and the two angles next to it · SsA: two sides and the angle opposite the longer side

Triangle inequality: two sides together are always longer than the third.

Sides and angles: the larger angle lies opposite the longer side.

AAA is not a congruence theorem: three angles only fix the shape, not the size.

Labelling: the side $a$ lies opposite the vertex $A$, the side $b$ opposite the vertex $B$, the side $c$ opposite the vertex $C$.

INTERACTIVE · WHICH PARTS FIX THE TRIANGLE?

Choose three parts and see whether there is no triangle, exactly one or two different ones.

INTERACTIVE · THREE STICKS

Change the three side lengths. When does the triangle close? Where is the largest angle?

EXAMPLE 5 · DOES THE TRIANGLE EXIST?

Can you draw a triangle with 3 cm, 5 cm and 9 cm?

The two shorter sides: $3 + 5 = 8$. That is shorter than 9.

No, there is no triangle.

EXAMPLE 6 · CONSTRUCTION BY SSS

Construct a triangle with $a = 4$ cm, $b = 5$ cm, $c = 6$ cm.

Draw $\overline{AB} = c = 6$ cm. A circle around $A$ with $b = 5$ cm, a circle around $B$ with $a = 4$ cm. The point of intersection is $C$.

Exactly one triangle (above or below is the same, just reflected).

EXERCISES

Is there a triangle? a) 4 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm   b) 2 cm, 3 cm, 6 cm   c) 3 cm, 4 cm, 7 cm   d) 6 cm, 6 cm, 6 cm

a) yes   b) no   c) no, $3 + 4 = 7$ only gives a flat line segment   d) yes, equilateral

Which congruence theorem fits? a) $a$, $b$, $c$   b) $c$, $\alpha$, $\beta$   c) $a$, $b$, $\gamma$   d) $b$, $c$ with $c > b$ and $\gamma$

a) SSS   b) ASA   c) SAS   d) SsA

Construct a triangle with $c = 5$ cm, $\alpha = 40°$, $\beta = 60°$. Measure $\gamma$ and check with the angle sum theorem.

ASA. You get $\gamma = 80°$, because $180° - 40° - 60° = 80°$.

Two sides of a triangle are 5 cm and 8 cm long. Between which values does the third side lie?

Longer than $8 - 5 = 3$ cm and shorter than $8 + 5 = 13$ cm.

In a triangle, $\beta = 80°$ and $\gamma = 40°$. Put the sides in order of length without drawing.

$\alpha = 60°$. Largest angle $\beta$, so longest side $b$; smallest angle $\gamma$, so shortest side $c$: $c < a < b$.

TEST YOURSELF!

Two sides are 5 cm and 8 cm. Below which length in cm must the third side stay?

$5 + 8 = 13$

$c = 5$ cm, $\alpha = 40°$, $\beta = 60°$. How big does $\gamma$ become?

$180° - 100° = 80°$

An isosceles triangle has a base of 10 cm. Longer than how many cm must each leg be?

The two legs together longer than 10 cm, so each longer than 5 cm.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

In a triangle, $\alpha = 47°$ and $\beta$ is twice as big as $\alpha$. Calculate $\gamma$.

$\beta = 94°$, $\gamma = 180° - 141° = 39°$.

From home to school it is 3 km as the crow flies, from school to the sports ground 2 km. How far can it be from home to the sports ground at most and at least?

At most $3 + 2 = 5$ km, at least $3 - 2 = 1$ km (if everything lies on one line).

Given are $a = 6$ cm, $b = 6$ cm and $\gamma = 60°$. Which special triangle do you get? Give a reason without drawing.

Isosceles, so $\alpha = \beta = (180° - 60°) : 2 = 60°$. All angles 60°: equilateral, so $c = 6$ cm as well.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Euclid and the proof of the angle sum

That the angles in a triangle add up to two right angles was already known to the Greeks. Around 300 BC in Alexandria, the mathematician Euclid wrote the “Elements”, a textbook in 13 books that was used at schools and universities for almost 2000 years.

In the first book, proposition 32 is exactly our angle sum theorem. Euclid proves it with a parallel line – with the same alternate and corresponding angles that you have met in this chapter. The congruence theorems SAS, SSS and ASA can also be found there (propositions 4, 8 and 26).

Try it yourself: Draw a triangle, extend the side $\overline{AB}$ beyond $B$ and measure the angle outside at $B$. Compare it with $\alpha + \gamma$.

The exterior angle is $180° - \beta$, and that is exactly $\alpha + \gamma$. This is also in Euclid’s proposition 32.

Source: Euclid, Elements, Book I, proposition 32 (angle sum and exterior angle), propositions 4, 8 and 26 (congruence theorems), around 300 BC.
